book: Chapter 7 · The Scope of Architectural Characteristics
title: Where One Set Ends and the Next Begins
gist: The old frameworks assumed one set of characteristics for a whole system. Modern architectures don't work that way. The architecture quantum is the unit that fixes this — and it turns out to be the thing that chooses your style for you.
minute: The fatal flaw in older approaches: **one set of characteristics for the entire system**. A microservices architecture has different characteristics at service level and at system level.

An **architecture quantum** is the smallest part of the system that runs independently: independently deployable, high functional cohesion, low external implementation static coupling, and defined at its edges by synchronous calls. Its database is inside it.

Four couplings, and they are not interchangeable. **Semantic** is the problem's own. **Implementation** is what you chose. **Static** is who must exist for whom. **Dynamic** is who calls whom while running.
**Higher coupling is allowed at narrow scope; the broader the scope, the looser it must be.** Tight coupling inside a service is cohesion. The same coupling across a shared contract is brittleness.
Scope decides style, in this order: how many sets of characteristics → monolith or distributed → quantum boundaries → persistence → synchronous or asynchronous.

sections.alt: A dashed boundary containing two services and their own database, with the four defining properties listed
sections.cap: Latin *quantum* — “how much”. Informally: the smallest part of the system that runs independently.
items: **Independently deployable** — everything needed to function is inside. If the application uses a database, that database is *in* the quantum, because the system doesn't work without it. Which means virtually every legacy system on a single shared database is, by definition, **a quantum of one**.

**High functional cohesion** — the quantum does something purposeful. In a monolith the cohesion is basically the whole system; in a distributed architecture you aim each service at a single workflow.
**Low external implementation static coupling** — the DDD preference for loose coupling between bounded contexts, one level of abstraction above components.
**Synchronous communication** — the calls between quanta are where operational characteristics collide.
sections.p: Code-level metrics can't measure scope. They tell you about the code and say nothing about the dependent things outside it — and no amount of designing a codebase to be elastic helps if its database isn't.

sections.alt: Four columns defining semantic, implementation, static and dynamic coupling
sections.cap: Static defines scope. Dynamic defines what happens when the scopes have to talk.
sections.p: **Semantic coupling** is inherent in the problem: an order-processing system couples carts to inventory to customers because the business does. No architecture pattern prevents a change in the domain from rippling — a change to the semantics *is* a change to the requirements. **Implementation coupling** is everything you decided: one database or several, monolith or distributed. It barely touches the semantics and it determines the architecture.
quotes: Higher coupling is allowed for narrower scopes; the broader the scope, the looser the coupling should be.

An architecture is *brittle* when one implementation change ripples out and breaks apparently unrelated things. Renaming `State` to `StateCode` should affect one caller — the moment it affects nine, the scope was too broad for that much coupling.

sections.t: Bounded context, and why shared entities failed
sections.alt: Tight coupling inside one boundary beside loose coupling between two boundaries
sections.cap: Each domain gets its own Customer, and the differences get reconciled at the points where they talk.
sections.p: Before domain-driven design, architects chased holistic reuse: one `Customer` class for the whole organisation. It produced tight coupling, harder coordination and more complexity. Eric Evans's **bounded context** says the opposite — everything about a portion of the domain is visible inside it and opaque outside it. Entities work best in a local context, and you pay a small reconciliation cost at the seams instead of a permanent coupling cost everywhere.

sections.t: Auction ends. Payment handles one every 500 ms.
sections.alt: A synchronous call from Auction to Payment failing, above the same call buffered by a queue
sections.sit: Two services in a microservices architecture. When an auction closes, **Auction** sends payment information to **Payment**. Payment can process one payment every 500 ms. A thousand auctions are scheduled to end at the same moment.
opts: Call Payment synchronously — it's a simple request.
The first call works. Then Payment cannot absorb the rate, and the rest fail. The two services have genuinely different operational characteristics and a synchronous call forces them to share one.
The queue is a buffer, and the two services get to operate at their own scale. Bursts are held until the receiver is ready.
sections.verdict: **Synchronous communication is unforgiving in distributed architectures**, especially where quanta have different characteristics — because a sync call makes the caller inherit the callee's limits. Async is not a free pass: sustained overproduction eventually overflows the queue too. It converts a *burst* problem into a *capacity* problem, which is a much better problem.

sections.alt: A decision tree from how many sets of characteristics through to synchronous or asynchronous communication
sections.cap: Fig. 7-1 · run this before picking a style, not after.
items: **One set of characteristics will do** → monolithic, and the number of subsequent decisions collapses. One database, developed and deployed in lockstep with the architecture. Done.
**More than one set** → distributed, and now you owe answers on quantum boundaries and on data: a single shared database (common in event-driven) or partitioned along service lines (microservices).
**Then the communication question.** Choosing synchronous can *move* the quantum boundaries you established through static coupling — the two kinds of coupling interact constantly.

sections.t: Going Green: one system, or three?
sections.alt: Three dashed quantum boundaries around the public-facing, back-office and assessment parts of Going Green
sections.sit: A business that buys, recycles and resells old electronics through public kiosks and a website. Characteristics analysis produces three distinct clusters: public-facing needs **scalability, availability, agility**; back-office needs **security, data integrity, auditability**; assessment needs **maintainability, deployability, testability**.
opts: Build one system that satisfies all eight.

Possible, and difficult. These characteristics counteract each other — fast deployability is much harder when you are also holding auditability, and the kiosk UI needs a completely different scalability profile from the back office.
Use the clusters as the quantum boundaries.

Three quanta, each with one coherent set of characteristics. Using characteristic scope as a first guide to service granularity is how you find a good set of trade-offs rather than an average of bad ones.
sections.verdict: Note *why* assessment gets its own boundary: the business resells the highest-value devices, and new models arrive constantly, so the faster they can update assessments the more valuable the stock they can buy. That is a **business driver producing an architectural characteristic** — exactly the translation from Chapter 5, now deciding a boundary.

sections.t: Scoping when the operations aren't yours
sections.alt: A dashed boundary containing two services and their own database, with the four defining properties listed
sections.cap: Cloud resources encapsulate operational characteristics, which is convenient right up until you need to reason about them.
items: **Cloud as an alternate operations centre** — you run and orchestrate containers. Then you must consider the characteristics of the containers *and* the constraints the orchestrator imposes.

**Cloud resources as system components** — triggered functions, managed databases, provider building blocks. Then you are reasoning about the capabilities the provider advertises and hopefully maintains.
sections.p: Elasticity used to be won by hand, on physical hardware, by the previous generation of architects; now it is a configuration setting. The specific difficulties moved — provider availability, a wider security surface — but the shape of the job didn't. Analysing trade-offs is the constant.

source: Fundamentals of Software Architecture: An Engineering Approach, 2nd ed. — Mark Richards & Neal Ford (O'Reilly, 2025). Chapter 7: The Scope of Architectural Characteristics, pp. 95–106. The architecture quantum was developed for Building Evolutionary Architectures; bounded context is Eric Evans's.
